title: Metres Are Not Millimetres: Making the Compiler Check the Units

questions.question: What does a double record about the quantity it holds?
options: Its magnitude and its unit
Its unit, through the variable's name
Nothing: metres and millimetres, radians and degrees, seconds and milliseconds are all the same type
Its precision, which implies the unit
questions.explanation: A comment saying millimetres, a name like distance_mm, and a factor of a thousand written wherever somebody noticed one was needed are all promises nothing checks.

questions.question: Quantity is a template over a Tag with no members, never instantiated. What is the tag for?
options: To store the unit's name for printing
To carry the conversion factor to SI
To let the quantity be specialised per unit
To make Quantity<MetreTag> and Quantity<SecondTag> different types, so the arithmetic defined between two of the same tag refuses the rest
questions.explanation: It costs nothing at runtime: sizeof is one double, it is trivially copyable, and every operation is a function that disappears.

questions.question: Which operation on two quantities of the same kind returns a plain number rather than a quantity?
options: None of them
Multiplication, which cancels the units
Subtraction, since the units cancel
Division: a length over a length is a ratio, which has no unit
questions.explanation: Multiplication of two lengths is an area, which this system has no name for, so it is left undefined and a check in checks/ proves it does not compile.

questions.question: Everything a type system promises is a thing that does not compile, and there is no RC_CHECK for that. How does this lesson test its refusals?
options: It does not; the refusals are documented instead
Snippets in checks/ are compiled by the build and the tests are marked WILL_FAIL, so a snippet that starts compiling is a test failure
By reading the compiler's output for expected diagnostics
With static_assert in the test file
questions.explanation: Keep each snippet to one refusal, since a file that fails for two reasons still passes when one of them stops working. And compile them against the finished implementation, or they pass for the wrong reason.

questions.question: A person's height and a wavelength of light are both Metres, and adding them compiles. Is that a hole in the design?
options: Yes, the constructor should range check
No: a unit type checks that two quantities are of the same kind, not that they are of the same thing
No, because the result is still a valid length
Yes, the tags should distinguish scales
questions.explanation: The same applies to frames, to ranges, to sign conventions and to sensibleness. degrees(370.0) is a perfectly good Radians and nothing here wraps it, because wrapping is a decision about meaning.

questions.question: Frame confusion is a real risk in a particular program. What does this design suggest?
options: More tags: Quantity<WorldMetreTag> and Quantity<BodyMetreTag> are two empty structs and one conversion that has to be called
A runtime frame field checked on every operation
Nothing; frames are outside what a unit system can do
Naming conventions, since types cannot express frames
questions.explanation: A type can only enforce a distinction you actually made in the type. Deciding which distinctions are worth making is design, and it is the part the compiler cannot do.
